hints: Start by picturing the journey - blood has just picked up oxygen in the lungs and is coming back to the heart. Which side of the heart deals only with oxygenated blood, and which chamber does it fill first?
Think about the order of pumping - the top chambers contract first to push blood down, then the thick-walled bottom chambers contract powerfully. What is this sequence called?
Remember valves only open one way and only when pressure behind them is higher. What must happen to ventricular pressure during contraction to first shut one valve and then open another?
Name the vessel that brings blood from the lungs to the heart and the large vessel that carries blood away to the body. Be precise with left side names.

Link the two left-side valves to pressure differences - the bicuspid valve closes when ventricle pressure exceeds atrial pressure, and the aortic semilunar valve opens when ventricle pressure exceeds aortic pressure.
walkthrough:
Follow the Oxygenated Blood Into the Left Side**
Blood returning in the pulmonary circulation is oxygenated. It enters the left atrium through the pulmonary veins. From there it flows down into the left ventricle. Keep everything on the left side - the right side handles deoxygenated blood, so mixing sides loses marks.

Get the Pump Sequence Right**
First the atria contract together in atrial systole, pushing blood from left atrium to left ventricle. Then the ventricles contract together in ventricular systole. This order matters because ventricular contraction is what builds up the high pressure needed to drive blood into the systemic circulation.

Use Pressure to Explain Valves**
Valves do not open and close by themselves. They respond to pressure gradients. As the left ventricle contracts, its pressure rises above left atrial pressure, forcing the bicuspid (mitral / left atrioventricular) valve shut to prevent backflow. Pressure keeps rising until ventricular pressure is higher than pressure in the aorta, forcing the aortic semilunar valve open so blood is ejected into the aorta.

Final answer: Oxygenated blood enters the left atrium via the pulmonary veins, then flows to the left ventricle. Atrial systole is followed by ventricular systole, increasing ventricular pressure. This closes the bicuspid / left atrioventricular valve when ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, and opens the aortic semilunar valve when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, so blood exits via the aorta to the systemic circulation.

hints: Look closely at Fig. 6.1 - you can see four folded blobs packed together in different shades. Remember quaternary structure means the number and types of polypeptides assembled together.
Now think one level deeper - what small non-protein part sits inside each folded chain, and what weak bonds hold the four chains to each other in the complete molecule?
walkthrough:
Count the Building Blocks**
Quaternary structure is about how polypeptides fit together. Haemoglobin is globular and made of four subunits - two identical alpha (a) globins and two identical beta (b) globins. That 2 + 2 pattern is what you can see as the different shaded regions in Fig. 6.1.

Add the Haem and the Holding Bonds**
Each of the four polypeptides encloses one haem group with $Fe^{2+}$. The four subunits are not joined by peptide bonds. They are held in the precise 3D assembly by hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions and ionic bonds between chains.

Final answer: Haemoglobin consists of four polypeptides: two identical alpha chains and two identical beta chains. Each chain contains one haem group, and the chains are held together by hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions and ionic bonds.

hints: Zoom in on where oxygen actually attaches - it does not bind to the amino acids themselves. Which metal ion inside each haem group is the reversible binding site?
For full saturation, think about how many binding sites the whole molecule has in total and what happens after the first oxygen binds to make the others bind more easily.
walkthrough:
Bind at the Iron**
Each haem group contains one $Fe^{2+}$ ion. One oxygen molecule binds reversibly to each $Fe^{2+}$. So it is wrong to say oxygen binds to the polypeptide - the binding site is the iron in haem.

Reach Full Saturation by Cooperative Binding**
Because there are four haems per molecule, full saturation means four $O_2$ molecules bound per haemoglobin. Binding is cooperative - binding of the first $O_2$ changes shape from the tense (T) to relaxed (R) state, making it easier for the 2nd, 3rd and 4th $O_2$ to bind, forming oxyhaemoglobin. This occurs readily at high partial pressure of oxygen, as in alveolar capillaries.

Final answer: Oxygen binds reversibly to the $Fe^{2+}$ / ferrous iron in each haem group, one $O_2$ per haem. A fully saturated haemoglobin carries four $O_2$ molecules, with cooperative binding as the molecule shifts from T to R state.
